Summary
Background Loss of Y chromosome (LOY), an age-related somatic mutation, is associated with various age-related
diseases, but its role in the onset and progression of Parkinson’s disease (PD) remains unclear. This study
investigated the relationship between blood LOY levels and the risk of PD onset and progression.
Methods We estimated the LOY level for each male participant based on genome-wide arrays or whole genome
sequencing data. We performed Cox proportional hazards regression analysis among 222,598 male participants in
the UK Biobank and linear mixed model analysis involving 2574 male individuals with PD across 14 cohorts,
encompassing 19,562 visits. In the Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) cohort, we further
compared brain structure using T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, and carried out brain
network functional connectivity analysis based on resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) datasets. Additionally, we
assessed the LOY status in single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) data, which included 1,303,531 cells
from 279 post-mortem samples across ﬁve brain regions, and performed temporal dynamic gene expression analysis.

Findings Male participants with LOY had a slightly higher risk of developing PD during follow-up (HR = 1⋅16, 95%
CI = 1⋅01–1⋅34, P = 0⋅04). Among males affected by PD, LOY carriers experienced accelerated neurodegenerative
progression, manifesting as more rapid motor impairment (P = 0⋅0072) and cognitive decline (P = 0⋅0005)
compared to non-LOY carriers. Patients with PD carrying LOY also exhibited decreased network functional
connectivity in certain brain regions. Notably, LOY cells were particularly enriched in microglia/immune and
vascular/epithelial cells, and a subset of genes in LOY-Mic P2RY12 cells were associated with PD progression.
Interpretation This data-driven study highlights the potential association of LOY with the onset and progression of PD
through the analysis of multi-scale data, including clinical phenotypes, brain neuroimaging maps, and molecular
proﬁles from single-nucleus transcriptome across multi-brain regions. These ﬁndings suggest that LOY may be an
accomplice to the onset and progression of PD.

Ageing

number of PD cases. Individuals living with PD expe-

Research in context
Evidence before this study
To date, numerous studies have established the links between
genetic factors and the onset or progression of Parkinson’s
disease (PD), predominantly implicating autosomal and
mitochondrial variants. However, the role of gonosomal
variations, particularly Y chromosome alterations, in PD
pathogenesis remains underexplored. To investigate whether
loss of Y chromosome (LOY), a prevalent age-related somatic
mutation, is associated with PD onset and progression, we
conducted longitudinal phenotype analysis and single-nucleus
RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) to assess the relationship
between LOY and PD.
Added value of this study
This study provides the longitudinal evidence linking
haematopoietic LOY to PD onset and accelerated motor and
cognitive decline in male patients. By integrating snRNA-seq
data from over 1⋅3 million brain cells, we identiﬁed LOY-
enriched cell types (microglia, vascular cells) and dysregulated
pathways (HIF-1 signalling, apoptosis), mechanistically
bridging peripheral mosaicism to central neurodegeneration.
These ﬁndings establish LOY as both a biomarker of male
ageing and a contributor to PD pathogenesis.
Implications of all the available evidence
This analysis suggests that LOY may be an accomplice to the
onset and progression of PD, providing insights into the
genetic underpinnings speciﬁcally in male patients with
Parkinson’s disease.

substantial economic and societal burden in terms of
caregiving and medical expenses.3 The severity and
progression of motor and non-motor clinical features
vary among patients,4 and PD occurs 1⋅5–2 times more
frequently in males compared to females.1 Disease
presentation and progression in individuals diagnosed
with PD exhibit numerous disparities between males
and females,5 with these differences being a signiﬁcant
predictor of progression.6 Notably, female patients face
an elevated risk of dyskinesia development, whereas
male patients have a higher susceptibility to cognitive
impairment5 and speciﬁc difﬁculties in language pro-
cessing.7 Neuroprotective effects of sex assigned at birth
may contribute to the differences observed in neurode-
generative diseases.8 A recent study has reported that
hormones may play a differential role in the clinical and
pathological features of PD in male patients.9 Systematic
analysis of brain transcriptomic data from controls and
individuals with PD has revealed sex-related molecules,
pathways, and functional networks.10 To date, large
cohort studies have reported many genetic factors linked
to the risk or the progression of PD, focused on
autosomal11–13 and mitochondrial14 variants, but the ge-
netic association between gonosomal variants and the
risk or progression of PD remains to be elucidated.
Loss of Y chromosome (LOY) is the most common
somatic chromosomal variation in the human genome,15
typically associated with normal ageing,16 with preva-
lence rates reaching 40% among men over 70 years
old.17 Recent researches indicate that LOY has signiﬁ-
cant potential as a biomarker for disease prediction and
early detection.18,19 A recent ﬂurry of discoveries based
on advanced methods to identify LOY in large-scale
cohorts has revealed the associations between the pres-
ence of abnormal LOY in male blood and overall mor-
tality rate, as well as various disease risks: such as
cancers,20,21 rare autoimmune diseases,22 Alzheimer’s
disease,23 heart failure mortality,24 and metabolic health25
in males. Multiple large cohort-based epidemiological
studies have shown that LOY in blood cells is strongly
associated with increased susceptibility to various age-
related diseases, including both haematologic malig-
nancies and solid tumours.18,26,27 Although LOY has been
linked to various complex diseases, the speciﬁc mecha-
nisms underlying LOY occurrence remain unclear. In
addition to ageing, smoking in men may induce LOY,28
and a genome-wide association study (GWAS) of
205,011 males in the UK Biobank identiﬁed 156 com-
mon gene loci associated with LOY,17 and related to
peripheral blood cell counts.29 Another study of Japanese
men identiﬁed 46 risk loci associated with leucocyte
LOY, conﬁrming the relationship between LOY and
blood cell differentiation.30 However, to the best of our
knowledge, no studies have been conducted to investi-
gate the effects of LOY on the onset and progression of
PD. In this study, we collected the UK Biobank and
International
Genetics
of
Parkinson
Disease
Progression (IGPP) cohorts to analyse the relationship
between blood LOY levels and the risk of PD onset and
progression. Using T1-weighted magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) and resting-state functional MRI (rs-
fMRI) imaging data from the Parkinson’s Progression
Markers Initiative (PPMI) cohort, we examined the
changes of neuroimaging features in the male patients
with PD carrying LOY. Additionally, single-nucleus
RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) data from the Acceler-
ating Medicines Partnership PD (AMP-PD) allowed us
to map LOY cell distribution across 54 brain cell types
and identify LOY-speciﬁc genes linked to PD progres-
sion. Our exploratory analysis provides genetic insights
into Parkinson’s disease and may pave the way for
therapies targeting patients with PD carrying LOY.
Methods
Study design and participant
The design of the UK Biobank has been previously re-
ported.31,32 In brief, it is a population-based prospective
cohort of 500,000 men and women, aged between 40
and 69 at recruitment, which is reasonably representa-
tive of the national distribution for different ethnic
groups in the UK and is suitable to study a wide range of
middle-to-old age diseases, such as PD. We selected
223,289 male participants from a total of 502,142 par-
ticipants, excluding 120 individuals without follow-up
records, 557 participants who had a prior diagnosis of
PD at the time of blood sampling, and 14 participants
with unknown age. This resulted in an analysis cohort of
222,598 male participants (Supplementary Fig. S1).
The IGPP PD cohorts included in this study were
described in the previous works.6,12,14,33 The DNA sam-
ples in the Banner health study were from post-mortem
tissue, and these patients were removed in this study.
Brieﬂy, individuals with PD from North America and
Europe included 13 cohorts comprising a total of 2285
male patients with available genotyping data, and the
PPMI cohort comprised 289 male patients with available
whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data (Supplementary
Fig. S2). IGPP integrated distinct types of cohorts with
good representativeness of longitudinal phenotypes in
PD, including purpose-designed biomarker studies,
phase 3 clinical trials, and population-based prospective
cohorts. Individuals were diagnosed with Parkinson’s
disease according to the modiﬁed diagnostic criteria of
the UK Parkinson’s Disease Society Brain Bank. Here,
genotyping arrays or WGS were performed on DNA
from peripheral blood. It should be noted that the
samples from IGPP containing 13 cohorts utilised the
Illumina
Inﬁnium
Multi-Ethnic
Genotyping
Array
(MEGA).34 We ﬁltered out samples with a standard de-

Estimation of LOY carrier
For the UK Biobank cohort, we utilised genome-wide
arrays containing 691 markers spanning male-speciﬁc
regions
of
the
Y
chromosome
(MSY)
(chrY:
2,658,271–2,876,492,
hg19/GRCh37,
Supplementary
Fig. S1). For each participant, reported LRR and B
allele frequency (BAF) were available. The LRR was
employed to detect Y chromosome mosaicism, as it is
a standardised measure of total signal intensity that
provides relative copy number data. We assessed each
participant’s deviation from the expected median LRR
(mLRR) to identify evidence of loss in the MSY. Evi-
dence of loss is indicated by negative mLRR values,
while evidence of gain is indicated by positive mLRR
values. A left threshold based on the 99% conﬁdence
interval was utilized as a cutoff, designating samples
below this threshold as LOY carriers, while the
remaining samples were classiﬁed as non-LOY car-
riers23; We used the median LRR in the MSY (mLRRY)
threshold
of
−0⋅08
(Supplementary
Fig.
S1a)
to
represent LOY in approximately 10⋅49% of cells,
calculated using the formula: LOY (%) = 100 × (1 – 22 ×
mLRRY).35
For the PPMI cohort, which only included WGS
data, we applied a statistical approach (moCha)36,37 to
identify male individuals with LOY. A previous study
has compared moChA and mLRRY methods based on
the sample size and the ratio of genotyped pseudoau-
tosomal region 1 (PAR1) to non-PAR SNPs on the Y
chromosome.17 The moCha leverages long-range phase
information to detect localised disparities in allelic
fractions between maternal and paternal contributions
within a population of cells. By doing so, it improves the
sensitivity for detecting signiﬁcant events that occur at
low cell fractions. Additionally, it enables the analysis of
allele-speciﬁc genotyping intensities within the PAR of
the sex chromosomes, further enhancing its utility.
For the IGPP cohort, genome-wide arrays containing
3895 markers on the Y chromosome provided sufﬁcient
power for LOY identiﬁcation using the mLRRY and
moCha methods (Supplementary Fig. S2d). We used the
mLRRY threshold of −0⋅05 (Supplementary Fig. S2a) to
represent LOY in approximately 6⋅69% of cells, calculated
using the formula: LOY (%) = 100 × (1 – 22 × mLRRY).35
Imaging
Participants and MRI acquisition
Based on the moCha results of classifying PPMI male
participants into LOY and non-LOY carriers, 283 in-
dividuals (LOY carriers, n = 51, non-LOY carriers,
n = 232) diagnosed with PD who had undergone T1-
weighted MRI scans were included in anatomical im-
age analysis. For the functional image analysis, we
included 83 individuals (LOY carriers, n = 12, non-LOY
carriers, n = 71) diagnosed with PD who had undergone
rs-fMRI scans. It should be noted that most of the pa-
tients in PPMI were early, untreated sporadic PD.
We collected demographic characteristics (i.e., age at
baseline, years of education, and disease duration) and
clinical scales, including MDS-UPDRS II-III, Montreal
Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), Geriatric Depression
Scale (GDS), and Hoehn and Yahr (H&Y) stage. Base-
line T1-weighted MRI scans, ﬁrst rs-fMRI and corre-
sponding T1-weighted MRI scans (0–4 years from
baseline) for each participant were obtained from the
PPMI database in September 2024.
The T1-weighted MRI scans were acquired using
3⋅0 T Siemens Magnetom scanners (Trio-A-Tim, Verio,
or Prisma) with a slice thickness of 1 mm. The rs-fMRI
series were conducted in interleaved acquisition mode
following
this
protocol:
TR
=
2400
ms,
echo
time = 25⋅0 ms, voxel size = 3⋅3 × 3⋅3 × 3⋅3 mm, and
slice thickness 3⋅3 mm. The acquisition time was 8 min
and 24 s, containing 210 time points composed of 40
axial slices each. (Detailed imaging protocols can be
found
at
https://www.ppmi-info.org/study-design/
research-documents-and-sops).
T1-weighted MRI scan analysis
The voxel-based morphometry (VBM) technique imple-
mented in the Computational Anatomy Toolbox12
(CAT12)
(http://www.neuro.uni-jena.de/cat/,
version
8⋅1) within the Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM12;
https://www.ﬁl.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm/software/spm12/,
version 7771) using MATLAB (version 2020a). Pre-
processed T1-weighted MRI scans with the default set of
parameters, including Diffeomorphic Anatomic Regis-
tration Through Exponentiated Lie Algebra Algorithm
(DARTEL) normalisation and modulation for nonlinear
components.38
Based
on
the
VBM
technique,
we
generated the density images of grey matter (GM), white
matter (WM), and cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) for each T1-
weighted MRI scan and then smoothed these images
with an eight-mm kernel. We also computed the total
volumes of GM, WM, CSF, and the total intracranial
volume (TIV) for each subject. Assessment of the quality
of MRI processing and segmentation by a quality
assurance check using the “Check homogeneity func-
tion” in CAT12. Grey matter volumes of the LOY and
non-LOY groups were compared using a two-sample t-
test, corrected for age at baseline, years of education,
and TIV. The P < 0⋅05 false discovery rate (FDR)
correction threshold was applied for VBM analyses.

(RRID: SCR_009550) release 22⋅v2407. Functional and

of a cluster-forming P < 0⋅001 voxel-level threshold and
P-FDR <0⋅05 cluster-size threshold.
Single-nucleus RNA-seq data preprocessing
The snRNA-seq data were obtained from the AMP-PD
project. One-hundred post-mortem individuals diag-
nosed with PD or controls were carefully selected to
represent the entire spectrum of PD neuropathological
severity and diverse clinical symptoms. The snRNA-seq
was generated from ﬁve brain regions corresponding to
different stages of the PD pathology.46 In this study, 60
male individuals with 279 samples spanned ﬁve brain
regions: regions affected in the early stages of PD
(DMNX: dorsal motor nucleus of the Xth nerve, n = 55;
GPI: globus pallidus interna, n = 57), and regions
affected in the late stages of PD (PMC: primary motor
cortex, n = 57; DLPFC: dorsolateral prefrontal cortex,
n = 57; PVC: primary visual cortex, n = 53).
We used SCANPY47 (V1⋅10⋅4) for processing, clus-
tering, and inferring cell identities from snRNA-seq
expression
proﬁles.
Only
high-quality
cells
were
retained, and cells were ﬁltered based on the following
criteria: unique molecular identiﬁer (UMI) counts
(3000 ≤n (UMI) ≤110,000), gene counts (1100 ≤n
(genes) ≤12,500), and mitochondrial content (<2%).
Additionally, doublets were identiﬁed using Scrublet
(V0⋅2⋅1)48 and subsequently removed, resulting in a
dataset of 1⋅39 million cells across 279 samples within
ﬁve brain regions. Gene counts were normalised to the
total counts per cell, multiplied by 10,000, and then log-
transformed. Highly variable genes were identiﬁed us-
ing speciﬁc ﬁltering parameters (min_mean = 0⋅0125,
max_mean = 3, min_disp = 0⋅5), and these genes were
used to compute low-dimensional embeddings via
Uniform
manifold
approximation
and
projection
(UMAP, default parameters, using 50 principal com-
ponents and 15 nearest neighbours). Clustering was
performed with the Leiden algorithm (resolution = 0⋅04,
10 iterations), resulting in preliminary cell clusters.
snRNA-seq data cell type annotation
Cell type annotation was conducted using CellTypist
(V1⋅6⋅1),49 a logistic regression classiﬁer optimised with
the stochastic gradient descent algorithm. We trained
the model using an snRNA-seq dataset from the pre-
frontal cortex (PFC) of the brain, annotated as part of the
Religious Orders Study/Memory and Aging Project
(ROSMAP) project.50 The same quality control proced-
ures applied to our dataset were also implemented for
the ROSMAP dataset before training using the celltyp-
ist. train function. Subsequently, the trained model was
used to predict cell types and subtypes across the ﬁve
brain regions studied, based on celltypist. annotate
function with the parameter “majority_voting = True” to
provide consistent labels. The predicted cell types and
subtypes were further veriﬁed by comparing with

Discussion
To date, the large-scale genomic analysis represents a
promising way of gleaning the genetic underpinnings of
Parkinson’s disease, yet most works focused on auto-
somes, leaving the impact of chromosomal variations
outside this scope underexplored. Previous research has
identiﬁed common variants on the X chromosome
associated with PD risk,61 but a recent analysis of Y
chromosome haplogroups remains limited evidence
connecting Y-chromosome genetic risk to PD.62 In
contrast to the Y haplogroup from the paternal line, we
investigated somatic mutation loss of Y chromosome
(LOY) effects from large cohorts and proposed that LOY
may serve as a risk factor for the onset and progression
of PD. Based on the UK Biobank cohort analysis, we
suggested that higher LOY levels (indicated by lower
mLRRY value) are associated with a slightly greater risk
of developing PD (Fig. 1a). The observed association
between LOY and PD risk, although statistically signif-
icant, is modest in magnitude and should be interpreted
with caution. Here, we included various known PD
protective and risk factors, such as PD polygenic risk
score (PD-PRS), age, smoking, coffee, tea, and alcohol
consumption as variables in the Cox regression model.
Previous studies have shown that PD-PRS and age
signiﬁcantly inﬂuence PD risk,63 while smoking and
alcohol are protective factors,64,65 consistent with our
reports (Supplementary Table S3). Some cohort studies
suggest that coffee and tea may have a potential pro-
tective effect against PD66; however, we did not ﬁnd
signiﬁcant evidence for their protective effect, possibly
due to a reduction in signiﬁcance after adjusting for
multiple covariates. It should be noted that this analysis
showed that LOY, an age-related somatic mutation, is a
genetic factor for PD onset, independent of autosomal
germline variants (PD-PRS).
Age is an unavoidable risk factor for PD, signiﬁcantly
affecting LOY levels23 (Supplementary Fig. S1b and d).
To investigate whether age inﬂuences PD risk through
LOY levels, we conducted a causal mediation analysis
(CMA). Our results indicate a signiﬁcant direct effect of
age on PD incidence (excluding the mediating effect of
mLRRY, ADE (control) = 3⋅42 × 10−8, P < 0⋅0001)
(Supplementary Table S10, Supplementary Fig. S5a).
When accounting for the mediating effect of mLRRY,
the
effect

direct

(treated) = 3⋅43 × 10−8, P < 0⋅0001) showed a slight in-
crease, but the proportion of the mediated effect (Prop.
Mediated) was low, suggesting
that approximately
0⋅957% of the total effect of age on PD risk is trans-
mitted through the mediating variable mLRRY. Inter-
estingly, smoking is typically considered a protective
factor for PD,64 yet it signiﬁcantly alters LOY levels.28 We
also used CMA to explore the role of LOY in the rela-
tionship between smoking and PD incidence. The re-
sults revealed a direct effect of smoking (ADE (average))
of −3⋅5 × 10−3, while the mediating effect of mLRRY was
8⋅5 × 10−5. This indicates that mLRRY slightly di-
minishes the protective effect of smoking on PD risk
(Supplementary Fig. S5b, Supplementary Table S11).
In the multiple longitudinal PD cohort analysis, we
explored the effects of LOY on both motor impairment
and cognitive decline, using MDS-UPDRS III and
MMSE scores, respectively. It should be noted that the
HBS (Harvard Biomarkers Study), DATATOP (Depre-

Neuro-imaging exploratory analysis showed the LOY
group with lower functional connectivity across these
four brain networks and speciﬁc regions of the frontal,
occipital, parietal, and temporal lobes compared to the
non-LOY group (Fig. 3, Table 1). We hypothesised that
LOY, as an accumulating clonal haematopoietic muta-
tion, may inﬂuence the physiological activities of in-
dividuals with PD through various pathways. For
instance, LOY may affect brain function by altering the
strength of brain network connectivity rather than
directly impacting brain structure. The VisPeri network
in the LOY group with frontal and parietal functional
connectivity decreases, consistent with the idea of a
marked frontal-occipital-parietal dysfunction in the right
hemisphere.72 The salience network is coupled with the
default network, and the increased coupling within the
two networks can be observed across cognitive tasks.73
Consistent with previous reports, our results demon-
strated that the SFG, which is one of the typical regions
of the default network, showed lower functional con-
nectivity with the SalVentAttnA network in the LOY
groups when compared with the non-LOY group.74 The
limbic network is primarily concerned with the regula-
tion of emotion, motivation, and social behaviour.75 A
study shows that the functional connections between the
regions of the temporal-occipital visual cortex and the
prefrontal-limbic network were signiﬁcantly weakened
in patients with PD and depression.76 The reduction of
functional connectivity in relevant brain regions was
also found in the LOY group, which may indicate that
LOY
will
exacerbate
mood
deterioration.
Reduced
functional connectivity of the ContC network with
multiple brain regions may be associated with deﬁcits in
cognitive control, attention, and executive function.77
The pathological process of PD involves speciﬁc
brain regions.78 Lesions initially occur in the dorsal
motor nucleus of the glossopharyngeal and vagal nerves,
as well as the anterior olfactory nucleus. Over time, the
nuclear grey matter and cortical areas become increas-
ingly affected. We included single-cell transcriptome
data from 60 individuals across ﬁve brain regions cor-
responding to different stages of PD pathology, aiming
to understand whether and how levels of LOY in various
brain regions contribute to the progression of PD.
During the course of disease, microglia cells are acti-
vated not only in the substantia nigra but also in the
putamen,79 hippocampus, and cortex.80 They can trigger
neurotoxic responses in reactive astrocytes,81 interfere
with oligodendrocyte survival,82 and may contribute to
widespread neuroinﬂammation in the brain, thereby
mediating neuronal death associated with PD.83 In this
study, we identiﬁed a unique set of growth and
recession pattern genes in LOY microglia (Mic P2RY12)
cells (Fig. 4e), including genes related to the HIF-1
signalling pathway (FLT1, HIF1A, and PFKFB3) and
apoptosis-related genes (ACTG1 and TUBA1B), all of
which have been closely associated with the progression
of PD. Research indicates that the HIF-1 signalling
pathway inﬂuences PD through mechanisms such as
mitochondrial
dysfunction,
oxidative
stress,
and
impaired protein degradation.84 FLT1 helps restore
blood–brain barrier functionality by reducing neuro-
inﬂammation, potentially protecting neurons,85 while
HIF1A (hypoxia-inducible factor 1 alpha) contributes to
PD pathogenesis by modulating downstream gene
expression.86 Evidence indicates that microglial activa-
tion plays a critical role in PD progression.87 Speciﬁcally,
Mic P2RY12 cells, which function as homoeostatic
microglia, are implicated in the pathogenesis of nearly
all neurodegenerative diseases and have emerged as key
therapeutic targets.88,89 Furthermore, ACTG1 expression
in LOY Mic P2RY12 cells decreases with advancing
Braak stages, and the imbalance between ACTG1 and
GSTA2 may be a mechanism underlying cell damage in
PD.90 While previous research has shown LOY to be
enriched in microglia,51 we present evidence of LOY
enrichment in vascular/epithelial cells. However, given
the low proportion of vascular/epithelial cells in the
brain (1⋅35%; Supplementary Fig. S3b) and the limited
presence of LOY cells across various cell types (0⋅057%–
6⋅02% across seven major groups; Supplementary
Fig. S4a), we lack sufﬁcient LOY-vascular cells for
comprehensive analysis. Future studies should aim to
expand the sample size to better elucidate the role of
LOY in vascular/epithelial cell types. Taken together,
LOY cells in microglia may inﬂuence the progression of
PD in the brain by affecting various genes and
pathways.
Our study has several limitations. First, as LOY is an
age-related somatic mutation that may dynamically
accumulate over time, our cross-sectional assessment of
LOY levels at the time of sampling precludes analysis of
longitudinal changes in individual LOY burden and its
relationship to PD risk. Future studies with multi-
timepoint assessments of LOY levels may better delin-
eate its role in PD onset and progression. Second, our
longitudinal cohort analysis was restricted to patients of
European ancestry, replication of these ﬁndings in
ethnically diverse cohorts is essential to conﬁrm gener-
alizability. Third, the sample size (n = 83) in neuro-
imaging analysis is modest, and further independent
validation cohort studies are needed. Furthermore, our

In summary, this data-driven study highlights the
potential roles of LOY in male individuals with PD
through the analysis of multi-scale data, from clinical
phenotypes, and brain maps (neuro-imaging) to mole-
cules (multi-brain region single-nucleus transcriptome).
Our analysis results suggest that LOY serves not only as
a marker of ageing in males but also as a contributing
factor to the onset and progression of PD. A deeper
understanding of the mechanisms by which LOY level
inﬂuences PD could facilitate the identiﬁcation of bio-
markers and support the development of effective
therapeutic strategies for male individuals with PD.
